result: The authors assembled a high-quality chromosome-level genome of M. dirhodum using PacBio HiFi reads and Hi-C technology. The final assembly is 447.8 Mb with 98.50% anchored to nine chromosomes, contig N50 of 7.82 Mb, scaffold N50 of 37.54 Mb, and 18,003 protein-coding genes with 92.05% functionally annotated. BUSCO analysis showed 96.9% completeness, higher than several other aphid genomes.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm the genome quality, with one stating 'a chromosome-level genome of the rose-grain aphid M. dirhodum was assembled with high quality.' The editor's note confirms 'The current manuscript is significantly improved with additional data and clarification,' indicating acceptance of the genome assembly claims.

result: The authors systematically identified 11,678 A-to-I RNA-editing sites in M. dirhodum, with 62.7% in protein-coding genes and varying distributions across chromosomes. This represents the first systematic identification of RNA-editing events in aphids.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge this contribution, with one noting 'The authors present both genome and A-to-I RNA editing data.' Another reviewer states 'this study reports such an interaction in insects,' confirming the novelty. No concerns were raised about the RNA-editing site identification.

result: The authors identified two synonymous A-to-I RNA-editing sites on CYP18A1 that are closely associated with crowding-induced transgenerational wing dimorphism. Crowding increased winged offspring by 36.4%, while 20E treatment decreased it by 31.2%. The editing sites showed significantly higher proportions under crowding conditions, and CYP18A1 expression and 20E titer were altered accordingly.
evaluation: While reviewers acknowledge the findings as 'interesting,' one reviewer expresses concern about 'very small sample sizes' and notes that 'effect sizes in some comparisons (Fig 3J, 4A-C, 6E,H) are clearly not large, making confidence in conclusions low.' The editor notes improvements were made, but the initial statistical concerns suggest uncertainty about the robustness of these specific quantitative claims.

result: RNAi-mediated knockdown of CYP18A1 and ADAR2 decreased their expression by 51.4% and 46.7% respectively, reduced A-to-I RNA-editing levels on CYP18A1, increased 20E titer, and reduced winged offspring by 29.6% and 24.4% respectively. These results demonstrate that ADAR2 regulates CYP18A1 expression through A-to-I RNA editing to control 20E titer and wing dimorphism.
evaluation: Reviewers note the use of 'a wide array of molecular tools to identify connections upstream and downstream of the RNA editing,' but one reviewer raises concerns about small sample sizes and statistical reliability, stating 'effect sizes in some comparisons (Fig 3J, 4A-C, 6E,H) are clearly not large.' The editor's note about improvements suggests initial concerns were partially addressed, but uncertainty remains about the strength of these conclusions.

result: The authors identified that miR-3036-5p targets CYP18A1, and one synonymous A-to-I RNA-editing site (editing site 528) disrupts this binding. Under normal conditions, low editing levels allow miR-3036-5p regulation of CYP18A1, but under crowding, high editing levels prevent miR-3036-5p binding. Functional experiments with agomirs and antagomirs confirmed this regulatory mechanism affects 20E titer and wing dimorphism.
evaluation: Reviewers specifically highlight this finding as a strength, noting 'An interesting finding is that a A-to-I RNA editing site in CYP18A1 ruin the miRNA binding site of miR-3036-5p. And loss of miR-3036-5p regulation lead to less 20E and winged offspring.' This mechanism is central to the reviewers' positive assessment of the study's contribution.

result: ADAR2 transcriptional level was 2.19-fold higher in crowding + 20E treatment compared to normal conditions, but no significant difference was found between crowding alone and normal conditions, indicating ADAR2 expression is induced by 20E but not by crowding alone.
evaluation: One reviewer specifically mentions 'effect sizes in some comparisons (Fig 3J, 4A-C, 6E,H) are clearly not large,' directly referencing Figure 3J which presents this ADAR2 data. This suggests the reviewer questions the robustness of this particular finding despite the statistical significance claimed.

result: The authors conclude that A-to-I RNA editing is a dynamic mechanism regulating transgenerational wing dimorphism in aphids, representing the first report of RNA editing involvement in insect developmental polyphenism and demonstrating that insects use RNA editing to adapt to environmental pressure and generate phenotypic plasticity.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm this conclusion, with one stating 'this study reports such an interaction in insects' and another noting it presents 'an important finding on the molecular mechanism for transduction of environmentally induced polyphenism.' The novelty and significance of linking RNA editing to insect polyphenism is consistently recognized across reviews.
